prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: In C57BL/6J mice, the protein NeuN forms a stable gradient that separates the four different types of spiral ganglion neurons.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Quantitative measurements at 14 days, 2 months, and 12 months showed NeuN levels were highest in Type Ic neurons, medium in Type Ib, low in Type Ia, and missing in Type II neurons.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The amount of NeuN was inversely related to calretinin and positively related to Brn3a, indicating a smooth gradient rather than a simple on/off switch.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Experiments using four labels at once confirmed that the brightness of NeuN matched the neuron subtype defined by the combination of calretinin and Brn3a.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In 2-month-old mice, NeuN and calretinin varied significantly across the frequency map of the ear, while Brn3a stayed uniform.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Over the lifespan, NeuN and calretinin changed depending on their location, but Brn3a remained stable.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Even though hearing thresholds rose at 12 months, the differences in NeuN and its relationship with other markers were maintained.
facts.subject: animals
